title: Artificial intelligence literacy and innovative behavior among clinical nurses: the roles of AI self-efficacy and organizational innovation climate.
text: Objective To investigate the current status and related factors of innovative behavior among clinical nurses in tertiary hospitals and explore the relationships and pathways among artificial intelligence literacy, AI self-efficacy, organizational innovation climate, and nurse innovative behavior, for providing a basis for targeted nursing management strategies. Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted on 850 nurses from six tertiary medical institutions using a stratified survey approach in Yueyang city, Hunan province, from June to July 2026, in the General Information Questionnaire, Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale, Organizational Innovation Climate Scale, and Nurse Innovative Behavior Scale were used. AMOS 24.0 was used to conduct confirmatory factor analysis to assess the model fit of the scales. SPSS 26.0 was used for descriptive statistics, univariate analysis, Pearson correlation analysis, and multiple linear regression. PROCESS macro version 4.2 Models 4 and 14 tested mediation and moderated mediation effects. Results A total of 850 valid questionnaires were obtained, with a valid questionnaire rate of 95.3%. The mean nurse innovative behavior score was 37.93±6.50. The measurement model for the four scales showed good fit, and the scales demonstrated good convergent validity and some evidence of discriminant validity. Artificial intelligence literacy, artificial intelligence self-efficacy, organizational innovation climate, and innovative behavior showed positive associations with one another (r = 0.609-0.797, P < 0.01). Educational level, professional title, participation in research or innovation activities, artificial intelligence literacy, artificial intelligence self-efficacy, and organizational innovation climate were factors associated with nurse innovative behavior and explained 60.9% of the total variance. Artificial intelligence self-efficacy partially mediated the relationship between artificial intelligence literacy and nurse innovative behavior. The indirect effect was 0.322, with a 95% CI of 0.243-0.403, accounting for 52.90% of the total effect. Organizational innovation climate moderated the relationship between artificial intelligence self-efficacy and nurse innovative behavior (b = 0.051, P < 0.01). The index of moderated mediation was 0.041, with a 95% CI of 0.009-0.078. Conclusion AI literacy was closely related to nurse innovative behavior, with AI self-efficacy as a partial mediator and organizational innovation climate as a moderator. Nursing management may focus on AI competencies, application confidence, and organizational support.

title: Evaluating a Large Language Model for Emergency Triage Using Synthetic Clinical Dialogues: Toward a Multimodal Clinical Safety Framework.
text: Background/Objectives: Prioritizing patient safety through accurate emergency triage is critical during mass-gathering events such as Hajj and Umrah, where high patient volumes can significantly increase the risk of clinical errors. Although the Emergency Severity Index (ESI) provides a standardized triage protocol, it remains dependent on human judgment, while traditional artificial intelligence (AI) models often struggle to capture the nuanced clinical context embedded in patient narratives. To address this gap, this study evaluates GPT-5.2 using synthetically generated dialogues as a step toward a conceptual clinical decision-support framework that bridges structured electronic health records (EHRs) with triage interactions through clinical dialogues. By combining narrative inputs with structured physiological indicators, it explores the potential to support more informed clinical decision-making under controlled simulation conditions. Methods: To evaluate this contribution, we systematically assessed the role of clinical dialogues in triage performance using a balanced and stratified dataset of 1000 simulated Hajj-context scenarios. Results: The results demonstrate that incorporating clinical dialogues can significantly improve triage performance, with a 79.7% relative reduction in under-triage across all ESI levels. A more noticeable improvement was observed in high-acuity cases, with a 91.9% relative reduction in under-triage. In addition, the model achieved a high-acuity recall of 94.5%, highlighting its ability to identify critical "red-flag" symptoms that are often not captured in structured data. These findings suggest that narrative context may contribute to more accurate triage assessment and improved identification of high-acuity cases. Conclusions: Consequently, when evaluated within a controlled decision-support setting, this study suggests that large language model (LLM)-based systems may improve triage reliability and may contribute to safer triage decision-making in high-demand clinical environments.
